title: Elaborative Interrogation
content_html:
Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised facts into understood explanations.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” in the APS review — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter? Why did the Greeks respond this way?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this idea work? How does it connect to the next topic? How would you explain it to someone who has never studied the ancient world?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the text support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1

Fact: “Xenia — the code of guest-friendship — is central to the Odyssey.” Ask why: because in a world without hotels or embassies, travellers depended entirely on the hospitality of strangers for food, shelter, and safe passage. Ask why again: because a guest who was treated well would honour the host’s name and reciprocate the courtesy if the roles were ever reversed — it was a social contract enforced by Zeus himself (Zeus Xenios). Ask how: this explains why Odysseus judges every community he encounters by how they treat guests: the Cyclops is monstrous because he violates xenia (eating guests instead of feeding them); the Phaeacians are civilised because they follow it perfectly (gifts, feasting, safe transport home). Ask why that matters for an exam answer: it connects a specific Homeric value to both literary evidence (Polyphemus episode) and the wider question of what the poem teaches us about Greek society.

Example 2

Fact: “Greek cities used myth as a symbol of political power.” Ask why: because claiming descent from a god or hero legitimised a ruling dynasty and gave a city divine protection — Athens claimed Athena had chosen the city as hers over Poseidon, which is why the Parthenon sits at the heart of the city. Ask how: the myth was displayed in stone — the pediments of the Parthenon showed the birth of Athena and her contest with Poseidon, making political theology visible to every visitor. Ask why that matters: it shows that myth was not just story but active propaganda, and it explains why source questions about temples ask you to link architectural decoration to religious and civic meaning. Ask why the connection between art and myth matters for the exam: higher-mark questions reward students who can explain why a piece of material evidence was made, not just describe what it shows.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you’re covering conceptual material — not just listing facts. Particularly powerful with Classical Civilisation’s recurring themes: why xenia matters in the Odyssey, why Heracles’ labours were culturally significant, why Mycenaean citadels were built the way they were, and why myths were depicted on temple friezes. Build it into every lesson revisit. The exam rewards students who can explain the significance of evidence, not just identify it.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

Questions to ask

  1. Why is this true?
  2. How does it work?
  3. Why does it matter?
  4. How does it connect?
  5. Why now and not before?
  6. How would I explain this to a friend?
